arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Denezpi's counsel argued the Double Jeopardy Clause limits sovereign authority.
The government argued the side that brought the case committed two distinct offenses.
Justice Barrett questioned the assimilation of tribal crimes into federal law.
Justice Sotomayor asked about the control of tribal prosecutors.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Denezpi committed a violent sexual assault on the Ute Mountain Ute Reservation. He faced charges in both tribal and federal courts. The Double Jeopardy Clause generally bars two trials for the same offense. The core question is whether these two sovereigns exercise distinct authority. If they do, both prosecutions are legal.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the boundary between tribal and federal criminal jurisdiction. It determines whether individuals on reservations face dual prosecution for single acts. The result shapes the practical reach of tribal sovereignty. It impacts how federal prosecutors handle crimes committed by tribal members.
